'''''Populus fremontii''''', commonly known as '''Frémont's cottonwood''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Van Buren |first1=Renée |last2=Cooper |first2=Janet G. |last3=Shultz |first3=Leila M. |last4=Harper |first4=Kimball T. |title=Woody Plants of Utah: A Field Guide with Identification Keys to Native and Naturalized Trees, Shrubs, Cacti, and Vines |date=2011 |publisher=Utah State University Press |location=Logan, Utah, United States |isbn=978-0-87421-824-4 |page=412}}</ref> is a [[Populus sect. Aigeiros|cottonwood]] native to [[riparian zones]] of the [[Southwestern United States]] and northern through central [[Mexico]].<ref name=ucjeps>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=52463|title=Jepson Manual|chapter=''Populus fremontii'' subsp. ''fremontii''|publisher=University of California Press|year=1993}}</ref> It is one of three species in ''Populus'' sect.'' Aigeiros''. The tree was named after 19th-century American explorer and pathfinder [[John C. Frémont]].

==Description==
[[File:Populus fremontii ssp. fremontii 001.jpg|thumb|Leaf: ''Populus fremontii'' ssp.'' fremontii'']]
''P. fremontii'' is a large tree growing from {{convert|12|-|35|m|ft|abbr=on}} in height with a wide crown, with a trunk up to {{convert|1.5|m|abbr=on}} in diameter. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth when young, becoming deeply fissured with whitish, cracked bark on old trees.

The {{convert|3|-|7|cm|abbr=on}} long [[leaves]], are [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]] (heart-shaped) with an elongated tip, with white veins and coarse [[crenate|crenate teeth]] along the sides, glabrous to hairy, and often stained with milky resin.<ref name=ucjeps/> Autumn colors occur from October–November, mainly a bright yellow, also orange, rarely red.<ref name=ucjeps/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://extension.usu.edu/rangeplants/htm/fremont-cottonwood|publisher=Utah State University|title=Range Plants of Utah|access-date=2017-01-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118065754/http://extension.usu.edu/rangeplants/htm/fremont-cottonwood|archive-date=2017-01-18|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The [[inflorescence]] consists of a long, drooping [[catkin]], which blooms from March to April. The [[fruit]] is a [[Biological dispersal|wind-dispersed]] [[achene]], that appears to look like patches of [[cotton]] hanging from limbs, thus the name cottonwood.

The largest known ''P. fremontii'' tree in the United States grows in Skull Valley, Arizona. In 2012, it had a measured circumference of {{convert|557|in|abbr=on}}, height of {{convert|102|ft|abbr=on}}, and a spread of {{convert|149.5|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.americanforests.org/big-trees/fremont-cottonwood-populus-fremontii-ssp-fremontii-2/|title=''Populus fremontii'' ssp. ''fremontii''|publisher=American Forests|access-date=April 24, 2019}}</ref>

=== Subspecies or varieties===
Two subspecies are currently recognized. Some confusion due to hybridization with a Rio Grande subspecies of [[Populus deltoides|''Populus deltoides'' subsp. ''wislizeni'']] had originally placed this [[Populus deltoides|eastern cottonwood]] subspecies as a ''P. fremontii'' subspecies, but it was removed in 1977.<ref name=Eckenwal>{{cite journal|author=Eckenwalder, J.E.|year=1977|title=North American cottonwoods (''Populus'', Salicaceae) of sections ''Abaso'' and ''Aigeiros''|journal=Journal of the Arnold Arboretum|volume=58|issue=3|pages=193–208|doi=10.5962/bhl.part.29239|doi-access=free}}</ref>
*''P. f.'' subsp. ''fremontii'', with synonyms ''P. f.'' var. ''arizonica'' - [[Charles Sprague Sargent|Sarg.]] and ''P. f. ''var.'' macdougalii'' - ([[Joseph Nelson Rose|Rose]]) [[Willis Linn Jepson|Jeps.]] from California and west of the [[Continental Divide of the Americas|Continental Divide]]<ref name=Eckenwal/>
*''P. f.'' subsp. ''mesetae'' - Eckenwal., of arid areas of Mexico and west Texas, and widely planted elsewhere, generally east of the Continental Divide<ref name=Eckenwal/>

==Distribution==
The tree is native to the Southwestern United States and Mexico.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-taxon=Populus+fremontii|work=Calflora Database|title=''Populus fremontii'' (Fremont cottonwood)}}</ref> In the northwestern US it is only found in the state of Idaho,<ref>{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2026 |id=306544-2 |title=''Populus fremontii'' S.Watson |access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref> but it is widespread in every state of the southwestern United States including California, Nevada, Utah, and Arizona.<ref name="NRCS">{{PLANTS |date=2026 |symbol=POFR2 |taxon=Populus fremontii |access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref> It is also native to a few locations in western Colorado as well as disjunct parts of New Mexico and far western Texas.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Ackerfield |first1=Jennifer |date=2022 |title=Flora of Colorado |language=en-us |edition=Second |location=Fort Worth, Texas |publisher=Botanical Research Institute of Texas Press |page=780 |isbn=978-1-889878-89-8 |oclc=1350496037}}</ref><ref name="NRCS" />

In northwestern Mexico it is native to the states of [[Baja California]], [[Baja California Sur]], and [[Sonora]]. In the northeast it is found in [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], [[Coahuila]], [[Durango]], and [[Nuevo León]] and in just [[Mexico State]] and [[Puebla]] in central Mexico.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |date= |title=''Populus fremontii'' in Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. |url=http://www.worldplants.de?name=Populus-fremontii  |website=World Plants |language=en |access-date=10 May 2026}}</ref>

A riparian tree, it grows near streams, rivers, [[Spring (hydrosphere)|spring]]s, [[Seep (hydrology)|seep]]s, [[wetlands]], and well-watered [[alluvium|alluvial]] bottomlands at elevations below {{convert|2000|m}} elevation.<ref name=ucjeps/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_pofr2.pdf|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture|access-date=February 5, 2002|title=USDA Plant Fact Sheet}}</ref>

==Uses==

===Cultivation===
''P. fremontii'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]] and [[riparian zone restoration]] tree. It is used in planting for wildlife food and shelter [[habitat]]s, and [[ecological restoration]], larger [[native plant]] and [[wildlife garden]]s, and [[natural landscaping]] projects,<ref name=ucjeps/> windbreaks, [[erosion control]], and shade for recreation facilities, parks, and livestock.

Frémont's cottonwood was used in the past by settlers and ranchers for fuel and fence posts.

===Native Americans===
;Traditional medicine
[[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] in the Western United States and Mexico traditionally use parts of Frémont's cottonwood variously for a medicine, in [[basket weaving]], for tool making, and for [[musical instrument]]s. The inner bark of Frémont's cottonwood contains [[vitamin C]] and was chewed as an [[Scurvy|antiscorbutic]] - treatment for vitamin C deficiency. The bark and leaves could be used to make [[poultice]]s to reduce [[Swelling (medical)|inflammation]] or to treat [[wound]]s.

;Art
The  [[Akimel Oʼodham]] of southern Arizona and northern Mexico live along [[Sonoran Desert]] watercourses and traditionally used [[twig]]s from the tree in the fine and intricate baskets they wove. The [[Cahuilla people]] of southern California used the tree's wood for tool making, the [[Puebloan peoples|Pueblo peoples]] for [[drum]]s, and the [[Colorado River|Lower Colorado River]] [[Quechan people]] in ritual cremations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mojavedesert.net/trees/cottonwood|publisher=MojaveDesert.net|date=n.d.|title=Digital Desert: Mojave Desert}}</ref> The Hopi of Northeastern Arizona carve the root of the cottonwood to create [[Hopi Kachina figure|kachina dolls]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Padgett, Kenneth|title=Kachina Dolls|url=https://kachina.us/|website=Guide to Hopi Kachina (katsina) Dolls|access-date=September 8, 2015}}</ref>
